title: Inverse Functions
lead: An inverse function undoes what a function does. This section asks which functions have one, through the one-to-one property and the horizontal line test; finds an inverse from a formula and draws its graph from the graph of the function; restricts a domain where a function is not one-to-one; and defines the inverse trigonometric functions that way.
objectives: Determine the conditions for when a function has an inverse.
Use the horizontal line test to recognize when a function is one-to-one.
Find the inverse of a given function.
Draw the graph of an inverse function.
summary_html:
• For a function to have an inverse, the function must be one-to-one. Given the graph of a function, we can determine whether the function is one-to-one by using the horizontal line test.
  • If a function is not one-to-one, we can restrict the domain to a smaller domain where the function is one-to-one and then define the inverse of the function on the smaller domain.
  • For a function $\kf$ and its inverse $\kfinv,\ \kf(\kfinv(x))=x$ for all $x$ in the domain of $\kfinv$ and $\kfinv(\kf(x))=x$ for all $x$ in the domain of $\kf.$
  • Since the trigonometric functions are periodic, we need to restrict their domains to define the inverse trigonometric functions.
  • The graph of a function $\kf$ and its inverse $\kfinv$ are symmetric about the line $y=x.$

figures.original_caption: Given a function f and its inverse f⁻¹, f⁻¹(y) = x if and only if f(x) = y. The range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹ and the domain of f becomes the range of f⁻¹.
(a) The function f(x) = x² is not one-to-one because it fails the horizontal line test. (b) The function f(x) = x³ is one-to-one because it passes the horizontal line test.

(a) The graph of this function f shows point (a, b) on the graph of f. (b) Since (a, b) is on the graph of f, the point (b, a) is on the graph of f⁻¹. The graph of f⁻¹ is a reflection of the graph of f about the line y = x.
(a) For g(x) = x² restricted to [0, ∞), g⁻¹(x) = √x. (b) For h(x) = x² restricted to (−∞, 0], h⁻¹(x) = −√x.
The graph of each of the inverse trigonometric functions is a reflection about the line y = x of the corresponding restricted trigonometric function.
The graph of y = sin x + cos x.

exercises.prompt: Is the function $f$ graphed in the following image one-to-one?
Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=3x/(x-2).$ State the domain and range of the inverse function.

answer.solution: Use the Problem-Solving Strategy for finding inverse functions. $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{2x}{x-3}.$ The domain of $f^{-1}$ is $\{x\mid x\ne 3\}.$ The range of $f^{-1}$ is $\{y\mid y\ne 2\}.$

exercises.prompt: Sketch the graph of $f(x)=2x+3$ and the graph of its inverse using the symmetry property of inverse functions.

answer.solution: The graphs are symmetric about the line $y=x.$

exercises.prompt: Consider $f(x)=1/x^{2}$ restricted to the domain $(-\infty,0).$ Verify that $f$ is one-to-one on this domain. Determine the domain and range of the inverse of $f$ and find a formula for $f^{-1}.$

answer.solution: The domain and range of $f^{-1}$ is given by the range and domain of $f,$ respectively. To find $f^{-1},$ solve $y=1/x^{2}$ for $x.$ The domain of $f^{-1}$ is $(0,\infty).$ The range of $f^{-1}$ is $(-\infty,0).$ The inverse function is given by the formula $f^{-1}(x)=-1/\sqrt{x}.$

[T] The velocity V (in centimeters per second) of blood in an artery at a distance x cm from the center of the artery can be modeled by the function $V=f(x)=500(0.04-x^{2})$ for $0\le x\le 0.2.$ a. Find $x=f^{-1}(V).$ b. Interpret what the inverse function is used for. c. Find the distance from the center of an artery with a velocity of 15 cm/sec, 10 cm/sec, and 5 cm/sec.

answer.solution: a. $x=f^{-1}(V)=\sqrt{0.04-\frac{V}{500}}$ b. The inverse function determines the distance from the center of the artery at which blood is flowing with velocity V. c. 0.1 cm; 0.14 cm; 0.17 cm

[T] Use a calculator to evaluate $\tan^{-1}(\tan(2.1))$ and $\cos^{-1}(\cos(2.1)).$ Explain the results of each.

answer.solution: $\tan^{-1}(\tan(2.1))\approx -1.0416;$ the expression does not equal 2.1 since $2.1\gt 1.57=\frac{\pi}{2}$—in other words, it is not in the restricted domain of $\tan x.\;\cos^{-1}(\cos(2.1))=2.1,$ since 2.1 is in the restricted domain of $\cos x.$

exercises.prompt: [T] Use a calculator to evaluate $\sin(\sin^{-1}(-2))$ and $\tan(\tan^{-1}(-2)).$ Explain the results of each.

answer.solution: $\sin(\sin^{-1}(-2))$ is not defined, and a calculator reports an error: the domain of $\sin^{-1}$ is $[-1,1],$ and $-2$ is not in it, since no angle has sine $-2.$ $\tan(\tan^{-1}(-2))=-2:$ the domain of $\tan^{-1}$ is all real numbers, $\tan^{-1}(-2)\approx -1.107$ is the angle in $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ whose tangent is $-2,$ and $\tan(\tan^{-1}y)=y$ for every real $y.$

footnotes.html: The key gives about $92^{\circ}$ for $M=1.4;$ $2\sin^{-1}(1/1.4)\approx 2(45.58^{\circ})=91.17^{\circ},$ which is $91^{\circ}$ to the nearest degree.
The book’s panel for $\sin^{-1}$ draws the curve flat at the origin. Its slope there is $1,$ the reflection of the slope of $\sin x$ at $0,$ and the curve turns vertical at $x=\pm 1.$
